quoted_text:
如果基于BTC链上可以做类似于Zcash的隐私转账，长远看，对Zec隐私币的叙事不利。不过，短期和中期不用担心，毕竟出来还需要较长时间。

具体怎么来看：

推文是研究团队 Alloc Init 发的论文，主题是隐私BTC，目标是在比特币一层上做类似 Zcash 的隐私转账，且号称不用改比特币共识、不用软分叉。

大概方案是：

1.  把普通 BTC 存进去，变成一张加密“票据”（note）；

2.  转账时用零知识证明：链上只证明“这张票合法/没被花两次”，不公开发送方、接收方、金额；

3.  需要时再取出来，变回普通 BTC；

从这个机制看，基本类似于Zcash那套方案：加密票据 + 作废标记（nullifier）+ ZK 证明。

主要区别是：它不自己开一条链，直接把证明挂在比特币上，再靠独立索引器去验证。 

论文也承认有硬伤：

一是，进出通道还没做完（peg-in / peg-out）；二是，不保证存进去、取出来时隐私完好，进出仍可能被链上分析对上；三是，新池子刚开始人很少，匿名集很小；时间、金额、手续费、已知对手方仍可能暴露用户。

也就是，它还是早期概念，还不属于成熟产品。

对ZEC对影响：

如果顺利落地，真能在 BTC 上比较顺手地做隐私转账，一部分人就不必再换成 ZEC，会损失一部分玩家；更重要的是，叙事上，再打“隐私BTC”替代品就比较难了，对独占叙事有稀释。

不过，短期和中期，问题不大：

Zcash 已经在跑，且有成熟 shielded pool/有 ETF/有机构资金/还有 NU7（更快出块）等自己的升级，有ZEC自己的玩家群体。

短中期问题不大，长期的话，需要关注落地情况。

text:
⚠️ Bitget $387.5M hack: status update and security analysis

Bitget now puts the theft at about $387.5M, up from the first $351.6M figure. The increase adds Zcash and TRON. It is not a second raid. Compromised wallets were some of Bitget Exchange’s hot and warm wallets. Bitget says cold storage and the separately operated Bitget Wallet self-custody product were not hit.

This was not a private-key leak. It was another break in the transaction-signing trust chain. Attackers got Bitget’s own signing stack to produce valid signatures for transfers the exchange never meant to send, then those transfers confirmed. Same structural risk as the 2025 Bybit hack ($1.5B, Safe signing UI tampered): one signing pipeline, one trust root, an obvious target.

GoPlus has blacklisted attacker-linked addresses and shared the set with ecosystem partners to help freeze flows and cut residual loss.

I. Timeline

Sept 24, 18:31 — attacker receive address funded with 0.84 ETH for gas. The gas came from a Bitget hot wallet already under attacker control. Bitget says unauthorized transfers were detected the same minute.

18:58 — first large out: ~$34.75M USDT to the same address funded 27 minutes earlier.

19:16 — largest wave: ~$185M withdrawn in about a minute, including 13,966 ETH on Ethereum, ~91.4M XRP on XRPL, and 20.6M TRX on TRON.

18:58–21:23 — 2h 25m multi-chain drain window: ETH / USDT / USDC / AVAX / BNB / XAUt / XRP / TRX.

From 19:00 — attacker swapped stables to ETH via DEX and bridged the pile onto Ethereum.

~21:30 — Bitget CEO Gracy Chen posted the security notice and paused withdrawals.

~22:00 — ~$155M on EVM (ETH/AVAX) split into multiple “dormant vault” addresses.

Sept 25, 02:13 onward — continued splitting and movement. Trace: https://t.co/3JXFLp1cVu

Sept 26 — Bitget said root-cause work and system fixes were done and began reopening withdrawals.

II. Root Cause Analysis

Official update
Gracy Chen: attackers compromised a critical backend system in the wallet infrastructure, forged transaction data, and drove Bitget’s own authorized signing flow to move funds. Key leak ruled out. Full technical report and the exact intrusion path are still unpublished.

Structural root cause: signing pipeline trusts a single backend

Typical CEX withdrawal path: user request → backend checks (balance / risk / whitelist) → build unsigned tx → MPC / multisig / HSM signs → broadcast.

What broke: attackers bypassed backend checks and built unsigned txs that risk controls never stopped. The signer — MPC or multisig — cannot judge what it should sign. It signs whatever the backend hands it.

They did not take the key layer. They took the risk-decision layer. Once the “what to sign” data source was poisoned, every control sitting on that same backend — rules, limits, approvals — was skipped.

Supporting detail: the 0.84 ETH gas on the receive address came from Bitget’s own compromised hot wallet. Before the main drain, they could already drive the signing path. That was a dry run.

Forged data also explains the ~3-hour gap: “detected” at 18:31, last out at 21:23. Those transfers likely looked legitimate to internal monitoring, or the signing pipeline had no remotely triggerable kill switch. That delay needs a postmortem as much as the intrusion itself.

Possible initial paths (speculation, pending the official report)

▪️ Direct tampering / fake rows in the withdrawal database

▪️ Forged or replayed internal API calls (weak request-level auth / no replay protection between backend and signer)

▪️ Injection into the backend → signer message queue

▪️ Whitelist / address-map swap (user withdrawal address replaced with the attacker’s)

Compared with the 2025 Bybit hack

Bybit: Safe frontend injected with a malicious script. Signers saw one thing, signed another.
Bitget: backend data forged. No human “see” step. Automated signing just ran.
Same WYSIWYS failure, front-end vs back-end. Both incidents are being tied to DPRK clusters.

III. Attacker addresses and attribution

Bitget and the industry published primary attacker / first-hop receive addresses early, including:
0xA6dD3F218B65E32Ccc37BE30f74884133c655545
0xD2C2f029eFF5caCc686F24377CfdDcfc82d9F899
0x600cfeDc6Bd65Fa79B604dC44964f419e45784b2
0x94A43df7687A8494948Be937400e9d5D33135DA0
0x770b10b273fC44Fe9197D6bF20F145c2e98463Ee
0x7c96279Ec1e888Aa56b9B836e0dB26ca48573E1C

They have kept splitting and hopping to slow tracing and freezes. Related addresses are now near 900. More: https://t.co/3JXFLp1cVu

“Highly likely DPRK-linked,” on three layers:

▪️ On-chain links — researcher Specter tied bridged stolen XRP to proceeds from the July 2026 $24M AFX attack. Elliptic further linked this case to Bybit 2025 laundering addresses.

▪️ Off-chain signals — Bitget investigators matched IPs to a VPN pattern used by a known DPRK cluster (disclosed by Gracy Chen on an X live).

▪️Laundering pattern — stables / non-native assets swapped to native gas tokens within minutes to dodge issuer freezes. Classic DPRK playbook. Funds on Arbitrum were also jumped to Ethereum L1 fast, after the KelpDAO lesson: Arbitrum’s Security Council froze 30,766 ETH; Ethereum L1 cannot.

Note: Bitget has not published the technical basis for the DPRK attribution. Chen’s wording is “very likely.” High-confidence assessment, not a closed case.

IV. What CEXs should do now

1️⃣ Stand up an independent pre-sign risk engine
The failure mode: every control that trusted the business backend died with it. A separate system should simulate and score every tx before sign — size, outflow velocity, first-seen receive address, threat-intel denylist. “Tens of millions in one shot, brand-new receive address, several hot wallets firing in the same window” should have tripped any independent rule.

2️⃣ Circuit breakers and rate limits
Detected 18:31, last send 21:23. Almost three hours with no halt. If the first $34.75M had tripped a breaker, about 90% of the funds stay in the house.

3️⃣ People and supply chain
DPRK clusters live on social engineering, fake recruiting, and vendor compromise. Treat staff security, operational risk, and software supply chain as first-class controls, and reassess them on a schedule.

- Tokenomist: token unlocks and who gets the supply

- DeFiLlama: TVL, volume, fees and revenue
- Token Terminal: compare the numbers behind different projects
- Dune: dashboards for users and actual product activity
- CoinGlass: funding, open interest and liquidations
- Arkham: team, whale and exchange wallet movements
- TradingView: charts and strength against BTC
- Snapshot: votes on buybacks, staking and other proposed changes

so yeah, before buying any alts, see if there is any upcoming catalyst, check the unlocks, then see how much the coin has already moved.. and always check the original announcement for dates

@RBlinkyNYC  started the auction for The Last Flower #1 @networkeddotart 

🩷

Controls

R — Toggle rain on/off
S — Toggle sound on/off
P — Save image as PNG
I — Show information and controls
Click — Hear the sound and read the poem

The work is not an image; it is a weather condition.
Wind moves through the branches. The reflection beneath the surface breaks apart with the waves. Butterflies enter and leave at Fibonacci intervals. And rain — when summoned by the viewer — disturbs the surface of the water.
The poem appears and disappears line by line, like something remembered and then forgotten again.

The viewer is given a few keys. Everything else is left to the wind.

About the Code

The work is written in p5.js and is entirely generative.

The token hash is fed into a deterministic pseudo-random number generator. The same generator constructs the branches through recursive growth, plants the blossoms, selects the color palette, and determines the musical scale and tempo.

Sound is generated live rather than played back from a recording: filtered noise creates the textures of water, wind, and rain, while synthesized piano notes respond dynamically to the intensity of the wind at that moment.

The reflection exists as a separate visual layer, shifting line by line with the movement of the waves and wind. A layer of paper grain and ink texture is applied across the entire composition, giving the digital image the physical appearance of a printed work.

quoted_text:
WOAH! Nubank is in talks to buy Monzo for up to $13bn 

Once the darling of the UK fintech scene. Now an acquisition target.

Sky News reports early talks valuing Monzo at £8bn to £10bn ($13bn), about double its £4.5bn valuation in 2024. 

Its board is also weighing a new round above £8bn ($10.4bn) to fund a push into mainland Europe.

....

This hits different for me. In the UK. A Monzo customer. Having just met the CEO of Nubank last week.
 
Monzo has struggled with leadership changes and feature velocity. CEO TS Anil stepped down after a boardroom row last year, and ex-Google exec Diana Layfield took over in February.

....

Revolut, meanwhile, has 70m customers, a reported $115bn valuation and a full UK banking licence since March.

Monzo launched in the US in 2019 and has yet to establish a second market. 

....

What it does have is UK and EU banking licences, 15.2m customers, £25.7bn of deposits and deep integrations that would take years to build.

It makes a sensible acquisition target.

....

I find the strategy of this fascinating...

Monzo barely uses its balance sheet to lend. It held £2.3bn of loans against £25.7bn of deposits at its March year-end, so it lends out less than 10p of every £1.

Monzo would need much more capital to lend at scale. It still uses standardised risk weights, which make each loan more expensive to hold.

....

Nubank is the master of lending. It has a $39.4bn credit portfolio against $45.3bn of deposits, so it lends out about 87 cents of every dollar.

It could turn Monzo into something very different, with the capital and credit models to lend out far more of that £25.7bn.

...

Nubank also won conditional approval for a US bank charter in January. 

Monzo would add the UK and EU, right on Revolut's home turf.

It's about to get spicy between the big two.

....

Remember, these are early talks and Monzo declined to comment. It might never happen.

UK credit also pays thinner margins than Nubank's home markets, where its net interest margin is 22.9%.

...

Still. 🍿.

If Nu comes to Europe. 

European franchises have another thing to worry about besides Revolut.

shipping traffic, power prices, company revenue and compute demand are constantly changing

they already have a perp tracking the number of cargo ships and tankers moving through the Strait of Hormuz, updated every 15 minutes using live AIS data

if the data is reliable and liquidity comes, every valuable information stream becomes its own market

text:
有人把企业真实的 AI 模型消费数据拉出来看了一遍，结果和我们每天看到的 Benchmark 热度几乎是两个世界。

Tomasz Tunguz 的分析里，Anthropic 最强的 Fable 5.1 上线前 12 天，只占网关支出的 3.7%。大型企业账户中，前沿模型的 Token 占比也从 8 月的 53% 降到了 9 月的 45%。

更夸张的是 Cursor，基于 Kimi K2.5 微调 Composer 2，整体成本直接降了 86%。

我觉得这里真正值得看的，是企业开始按「每美元能买到多少智能」来选模型。

一个工作流要跑几十、几百次调用，模型只要跨过「够用」那条线，多出来的能力未必值得继续付溢价。接下来模型路由、微调和开放权重都会越来越重要。

Benchmark 在比能力上限，企业真正算的是每个工作流节点的性价比。

AI 模型市场最后最肥的那一块，可能恰恰是中间。

author: DavidDeutschOxf
quoted_text:
September 24, 2026: Noam Dworman sits down with "the world's leading famine expert" and reads him his old predictions and declarations about famine in Gaza.

Alex de Waal wrote the standard textbook on famine, runs the World Peace Foundation, and helped write starvation crimes into international law. When the media says "famine experts warn," this is who they mean.

In January 2024, he told Owen Jones famine would probably arrive by early February. February came and went. In March 2024, he told CBS it was expected between then and May. Days later, he told Democracy Now that children were dying "likely in thousands already." In April 2024, at Harvard, he called it the most intense famine since records began. In October 2025, Democracy Now brought him back.

Nobody ever asked him about any of prior predictions and declarations. On September 24, 2026, Noam Dworman did.

0:00 Alex de Waal admits to overstating catastrophes to get headlines
0:30 March 25, 2024. De Waal: The Famine Review Committee is "the ultimate arbiter, the High Court"
0:47 September 24, 2026. De Waal admits his own "high court" found no famine
1:11 March 2024: "It's too late to avert" thousands to tens of thousands of deaths
1:22 De Waal recasts it as conditional: "I said, yes, if this trajectory continues"
1:47 Dworman reads him the published wording, which was not conditional. De Waal: "We actually don't know how many have died"
2:14 Dworman to De Waal: You let Feroze Sidhwa tell my audience that 62,000 Gazans died of starvation
3:10 De Waal: We don't know the numbers. Dworman: The Gaza Ministry of Health doesn't claim anything close to your numbers
3:43 Dworman calls out the moving goalposts: "So I never said they were dying." De Waal accuses him of arguing semantics
4:21 Alex de Waal claims that the famine call "made no comment on the mortality"

—

What actually happened:

The IPC's own Famine Review Committee, June 2024: the famine claims were "not plausible," and "the available evidence does not indicate that Famine is currently occurring."
https://t.co/f85dKsV6gV

After the October 2025 ceasefire, a UNICEF-led survey found 0.5 percent acute child malnutrition in Gaza, one of the lowest rates in the region.
https://t.co/ysQqoYE9L1

Full interview: https://t.co/NfResC9KMs

--

In 2024, Alex de Waal was certain enough to tell the world it was already too late.

In 2026, Alex de Waal just isn't certain enough to say how many people died.

Alex de Waal once wrote that you need to overstate catastrophes in order to get attention. He was not joking.

Can an LM, starting from random init (!!), learn to generate all of its pretraining data?

Introducing Self-Play Pretraining with Zero Data. Two models start from random initialization: a generator proposes programs for a universal Turing machine and a learner trains on their outputs. We never train on any real data, but see predictable scaling on natural datasets: zero-shot val loss on images, text, audio, and melodies decreases predictably with self-play compute. And the learner develops in-context learning capabilities.

A fun proof-of-concept, co-led with @AdityaCowsik and @KfirDolev and co-authors @gbruno_dl, @ANourya @noahdgoodman, and @YoavLevine.

text:
The English translation totally lost the critical nuance of "温故而知新" in the context of Xi's private speech at the dinner. the onsite translator translated it word by word literally as "reviwing the past gives us new perspective" totally plain and neutral. But it often serves as a face-saving correction in the Chinese convo. Instead of bluntly saying, “You are wrong,” often time whoever use this word (in daily context likely used by the senior or whoever has the authroity) the speaker asks you to revisit the history and reach the intended conclusion yourself. It corrects you without publicly humiliating you. 

So the implied message here is something like:
“US China relations did not begin with your administration. Your government cannot simply disregard previous commitments whenever domestic politics change or a new president takes office.Your time as president is limited, so you should think carefully about the political legacy you will leave behind in US China relations. Do not squander the work of generations before you. To understand history is to recognize that neither country can pretend this relationship begins from scratch today.” 

In other words, it is both a reminder and a subtle warning. It's a really elegant and low key power play to scold someone without actually scolding them

@RBlinkyNYC  started the auction for The Last Flower #1 @networkeddotart 

🩷

Controls

R — Toggle rain on/off
S — Toggle sound on/off
P — Save image as PNG
I — Show information and controls
Click — Hear the sound and read the poem

The work is not an image; it is a weather condition.
Wind moves through the branches. The reflection beneath the surface breaks apart with the waves. Butterflies enter and leave at Fibonacci intervals. And rain — when summoned by the viewer — disturbs the surface of the water.
The poem appears and disappears line by line, like something remembered and then forgotten again.

The viewer is given a few keys. Everything else is left to the wind.

About the Code

The work is written in p5.js and is entirely generative.

The token hash is fed into a deterministic pseudo-random number generator. The same generator constructs the branches through recursive growth, plants the blossoms, selects the color palette, and determines the musical scale and tempo.

Sound is generated live rather than played back from a recording: filtered noise creates the textures of water, wind, and rain, while synthesized piano notes respond dynamically to the intensity of the wind at that moment.

The reflection exists as a separate visual layer, shifting line by line with the movement of the waves and wind. A layer of paper grain and ink texture is applied across the entire composition, giving the digital image the physical appearance of a printed work.

David Friedberg: Obama Doesn’t Understand AI and He’s Making Prosperity Political

President Obama last week:

“If we are thinking about AI just in terms of how do we cure cancer or get better energy, you can do that without having agentic AI. That's a misalignment between what our society needs and the commercial imperatives that these companies are facing.”

@friedberg:

“These words honestly just, they made me, like, emotionally distressed that if he's a leader that people listen to and he doesn't really articulate accurately what's going on, it's sad that we've lost the plot.

I think it's sad that we aren't all kind of holding hands saying, ‘My God, the future is here, and we all get to leap forward, and we get to bring people up.’

For years, Obama orated beautifully about the importance of bringing people up, about giving people the opportunity to progress, about letting people advance themselves. And there's never been a more equalizing technology, a better economic opportunity for prosperity for everyone than these technologies, than these tools.

And to hand wave the word agentic and say we don't need agentic AI to solve cancer shows how little he actually understands how this technology works and how it's all become just a shorthand for a political fight to what?

What are you fighting for? What is the political battle that says, ‘I am going to leave half the population behind, and I'm going to make an argument against prosperity for all, in order to make my party look like a morally superior party, and to cast the other side as bad when the other side has literally discovered fire and the world now has fire, and we're going to go take water and throw it on the fire.’

No one gets fire because the other guys are saying that fire is good.”

text:
WOAH! Nubank is in talks to buy Monzo for up to $13bn 

Once the darling of the UK fintech scene. Now an acquisition target.

Sky News reports early talks valuing Monzo at £8bn to £10bn ($13bn), about double its £4.5bn valuation in 2024. 

Its board is also weighing a new round above £8bn ($10.4bn) to fund a push into mainland Europe.

....

This hits different for me. In the UK. A Monzo customer. Having just met the CEO of Nubank last week.
 
Monzo has struggled with leadership changes and feature velocity. CEO TS Anil stepped down after a boardroom row last year, and ex-Google exec Diana Layfield took over in February.

....

Revolut, meanwhile, has 70m customers, a reported $115bn valuation and a full UK banking licence since March.

Monzo launched in the US in 2019 and has yet to establish a second market. 

....

What it does have is UK and EU banking licences, 15.2m customers, £25.7bn of deposits and deep integrations that would take years to build.

It makes a sensible acquisition target.

....

I find the strategy of this fascinating...

Monzo barely uses its balance sheet to lend. It held £2.3bn of loans against £25.7bn of deposits at its March year-end, so it lends out less than 10p of every £1.

Monzo would need much more capital to lend at scale. It still uses standardised risk weights, which make each loan more expensive to hold.

....

Nubank is the master of lending. It has a $39.4bn credit portfolio against $45.3bn of deposits, so it lends out about 87 cents of every dollar.

It could turn Monzo into something very different, with the capital and credit models to lend out far more of that £25.7bn.

...

Nubank also won conditional approval for a US bank charter in January. 

Monzo would add the UK and EU, right on Revolut's home turf.

It's about to get spicy between the big two.

....

Remember, these are early talks and Monzo declined to comment. It might never happen.

UK credit also pays thinner margins than Nubank's home markets, where its net interest margin is 22.9%.

...

Still. 🍿.

If Nu comes to Europe. 

European franchises have another thing to worry about besides Revolut.

author: GracyBitget
quoted_text:
THORChain and Stolen Funds: The Industry Needs Answers

After the $1.46B @Bybit_Official hack last year, nearly $1.2B in stolen funds was reportedly traced through @THORChain as the attackers moved assets across chains.

Today, following another major security incident at @Bitget , we are once again observing Bitget Exploiter funds being sent into the THORChain for asset swaps and cross-chain transfers.

The question is no longer:

“Does THORChain know these funds are associated with hackers?”

The attacker addresses have already been publicly flagged and are being actively tracked by exchanges, blockchain security/aml firms, and the wider crypto industry.

The real question is:

When a protocol is aware that funds originate from a publicly identified major hack, yet continues to facilitate large-scale cross-chain swaps, how should the industry view this under the banner of “decentralization”?

Decentralization should not become a blanket excuse when dealing with known stolen funds.

If, after every major crypto hack, attackers can continue using THORChain as a route to move funds from ETH → BTC, BNB → BTC, and across other chains, the industry needs to seriously ask:

What responsibility should THORChain bear when handling known stolen funds?

text:
I think $CHIP have one of the more overlooked business models in AI x crypto.

Much like $GRASS, the actual business goes beyond crypto and, IMO, sits in a pretty durable spot if hyperscaler capex, hardware churn and demand for compute continue anywhere near this pace.

Since their first ~$620K GPU-backed financing roughly a year ago, they've scaled remarkably fast to ~$611M deposited while reporting $14.3M in YTD revenue and a ~$30M annualized Q2 run-rate. Their June recap also cited $44.6M in protocol ARR (a bit confused by this part, but impressive).

They also just announced their largest financing in a $128.9M facility for 32 NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 systems backed by a multi-year contract with an investment-grade counterparty.

Why is this needed? Well, GPUs have traditionally been awkward assets for lenders because they depreciate quickly, hardware cycles move fast and underwriting them requires understanding the underlying compute economics.

ATM, only ~20% of $CHIP is circulating today, so the ~$480M FDV and eventual supply overhang are definitely major talking points, but the first major cliff isn't until April 2027, leaving a decent window to grow into the val before dilution matters.

I think this has a strong case for finding its way into everyone's rotation pretty soon. It sits at the intersection of AI capex, compute demand and has real revenue while the underlying business seems to be scaling fast.

Low float, real revs, narratively fitting, strong moat.

text: The long (and good) version of why today’s launch is a big deal for tokenized assets.
author: aave
quoted_text:
Borrowing USDC against Coinbase Tokenized Stocks is now possible on a dedicated @aave V4 instance on @base.

Coinbase Tokenized Stocks Spoke on @aave v4 lets users deposit stocks issued by @coinbase (AAPLc, AMZNc, GOOGLc, METAc, MSFTc, NVDAc, TSLAc) as collateral and borrow @circle USDC against them.

This allows users to keep their exposure to the stock without selling it while unlocking liquidity that can then be reinvested in other assets or spent, increasing capital efficiency.

Aave loans have no fixed term so users only need to keep a healthy LTV to avoid liquidation and they can repay the loan whenever they want.

In TradFi, borrowing against a stock portfolio means having access to a margin account that takes time and comes with account approvals, minimum balances requirements, and other broker terms

Aave v4 Coinbase Tokenized Stocks Instance reduces the complexity of this type of operation, opens access to more capital efficency, while leveraging onchain rails. At the same time, it brings more borrow demand for onchain assets that can pay a yield to users that want to provide liquidity to this market.

text:
The prevailing thesis is that onchain finance will transform brokerage, particularly lending and borrowing.

Aave has processed around $4T in deposits and $1T in borrowing, powered simply by onchain code.

Onchain rails enable faster, more accessible ways to trade, lend, and borrow by reducing reliance on intermediaries. Now its time to expand these benefits to stocks.

Over time, this has the potential to fundamentally reshape the cost structure of securities finance, creating more open, efficient, and deeper capital markets.

Excited to bring capital markets onchain, one asset class at a time.

author: zacxbt
quoted_text:
prompt for animated wizard 👇

Create a single self-contained HTML file that renders an animated pixel art wizard casting a spell, using vanilla JavaScript and Canvas 2D. No external assets, libraries, or network requests.

RENDERING
- Draw everything to an offscreen canvas at a fixed logical resolution of 128x96, then blit to a fullscreen display canvas scaled by the largest integer factor that fits the window, centered, with imageSmoothingEnabled = false and CSS image-rendering: pixelated.
- All drawing snaps to integer coordinates on the logical canvas. No sub-pixel positions, anti-aliasing, gradients, or shadowBlur.
- Fixed palette of ~24 hex colors: deep blues/purples for night sky, warm robe tones, 3-4 bright magic colors. Every pixel comes from this palette.

CHARACTER
- Build the wizard procedurally from filled rects and pixel runs, ~24x32 logical pixels: pointed hat with a bend, long beard, two-shade robe with darker outline, staff with a gem at the tip.
- Parameterize the pose (staff angle, arm raise, head tilt, robe sway). Animate parameters smoothly, then quantize to the pixel grid each frame so motion reads at an 8-12 fps pixel animation feel even though the loop runs at 60fps.

ANIMATION
- Looping state machine: IDLE (2-frame bob, beard sway) -> CHARGE (staff raises, gem flickers, sparks spiral inward) -> CAST (bright burst, projectile fires across the scene, 1-2 pixel screen shake) -> RECOVER (settle back). Ease pose parameters between keyframes.
- Pooled allocation-free particle system: preallocate and reuse. Sparks orbit the gem during CHARGE, explode outward on CAST, each particle stepping its palette index from white to magic color to dark before despawn. Snap particle positions to the grid when drawing.
- Fixed 60hz timestep update with rAF rendering. Zero object allocation inside the loop.

SCENE
- Minimal background: dark sky, a few twinkling 1px stars, moon, stone floor line. Character silhouette must read clearly.
- Subtle 1px rim light on the wizard from the gem, brightening during CHARGE and CAST.

QUALITY BAR
- Crisp pixels at any window size, seamless loop, stable 60fps, readable silhouette. Should look like a polished 16-bit sprite animation, not vector shapes scaled down.

text:
I’ve read the entire “Confidential Transfers” thesis from @SuiNetwork.

Here’s my honest take:

1. Public-by-Default has tradeoffs

Blockchains are transparent.

It's fine for traders and DeFi users who want to verify activity, but for businesses, that same transparency can expose a lot of information that they'd normally keep internal.

Things like:

→ Payroll amounts
→ Treasury movements
→ Supplier payments
→ Revenue flows

They can reveal quite a bit about the company and how it operates.

Businesses need the benefits of public settlement without exposing every financial detail.

2. Selective privacy > full anonymity

I agree with Sui’s approach here to keep balances and payment amounts private without making the whole system anonymous.

Businesses still need auditors, compliance teams, and issuers to access certain information when needed.

So the data stays private by default, with access still available to authorized parties.

That feels much closer to how businesses already handle financial privacy.

3. Confidential finance works better as a stack

A private transfer can hide the payment itself, but businesses also need to keep the systems around that payment private.

That includes things like payroll software, finance records, and rules for who can access certain information.

In my understanding, Sui is pairing Confidential Transfers with:

→ Seal for controlling who can access sensitive data
→ Nautilus for processing sensitive data privately
→ Gasless transfers for simpler stablecoin payment flows

This approach makes privacy a part of the whole flow, not just the transfer.

A much better setup in my opinion.

My takeaway:

Crypto-native users like you and me are already used to these defaults in crypto. It's a feature, not a bug after all these years.

I'm talking about things like public balances, visible transaction history, or separate gas tokens.

But they're not really optimal for businesses.

Finance moving onchain needs a middle ground, where it has verifiable settlement, more control over what becomes public, and fewer DeFi steps around the payment itself.

So I think Sui is getting that balance right with its confidential finance stack.

Better defaults make onchain finance easier to use, especially for businesses.

And it's a way for the crypto space to scale exponentially.

Disclosure: I’m a $SUI holder.

Okay. I’ll take the bait.

I went to work for Peter in 2013 with opposite politics.

He sat me down right at the beginning. 

PETER: “I don’t want the (Thiel) Foundation to do good that the market can do. That is the job of the market. Likewise, I don’t want to do the good work that is seen as good. That work can be done by people richer, weaker and more needy of approval than we are. I want us to do only the work that is *deeply* good but somehow confused for being evil, because that is the work of the courageous and the strong. We strive to be both and that is where a small foundation can make the greatest positive difference. Go look for such good and let’s do that. But remember. Good has TWO different  antonyms. What is “bad work”? It could be seen as shoddy work. Or it could be seen as evil work. And we can’t do shoddy work. Why? Because evil that isn’t competent never gets to be evil. It’s just pathetic. So we have to be exceptionally competent at the good work which we do to make sure it is always confused for evil.”

I thought it totally logical. So that’s the argument. And that’s classic Peter. 

This is an old idea of his. And now you know.

text:
扎克伯格对 Meta Muse 的思考真通透。

Meta 的 Muse 确实非常火。它甚至一度让我觉得，Codex 这类 Agent 会不会又变成了上一代产品。

这几天行业里关于 Muse 的分析已经非常多了。但如果大家真的对这款产品感兴趣，想深入理解，我还是建议去看一手资料。

扎克伯格刚刚参加了一期播客，详细讲了自己为什么要做 Muse，以及他对 Personal Agent 的理解。

我刚刚把这个视频看完了，绝对比市面上 99% 的第三方分析都更靠谱和通透。

怎么讲呢，我觉得 Muse 这种产品，确实有可能成为 AI 时代的微信。至少现在已经能看到一点苗头了。

咱一步步展开。

讨论这一切的前提，是得先搞清楚 Muse 和 Codex、Claude、WorkBuddy 等等这些过去半年竞争非常激烈的 Coding Agent、通用 Agent，到底有什么区别。

我反复看了扎克伯格的表达，如果用一句话总结，我觉得之前我们熟悉的 Agent，主要还是 Task Agent。Muse 想做的是 Long-lived Personal Agent。

Codex 已经是 Agent 了，这没有什么疑问。但它目前最典型的工作方式，还是围绕一个相对明确的任务展开。

比如我刚刚让它帮我改了一个产品 Bug，或者可以按照我的要求生成一份 Slides。

这类 Agent 的使用方式我们已经轻车熟路。给它一个任务，Agent 开始执行，最后交付结果。Meta 的 Muse 之所以能够出圈，是因为它在这个基础上，做了几个重要设计。

第一，它的生命周期更长。

这也是刚才提到的 Long-lived Personal Agent。

像 Codex 这种 Agent，虽然已经可以非常长时间地执行任务，但它的工作一般还是围绕一个 Task 展开。任务做完，这一轮基本也就结束了。

Muse 不太一样。用户给它的可以是一个持续很久的目标，然后它一直围绕这个目标工作。

扎克伯格举了个特别生活化的例子。他让 Muse 每周帮自己和女儿安排烘焙活动，还要提前把材料准备好。这周做完以后，这件事并没有结束。

比如这次发现 Cake Pops 太难了，他会把这个结果告诉 Muse，下一周再继续调整。所以这种任务可能持续几个月，甚至更久。

第二，也是我觉得最打动我的一点，它会主动观察用户，然后自己产生任务。

今天 Codex 这些 Agent 再强，大多数时候还是需要我们先告诉它要干什么。

Muse 有一个很重要的设计叫 Ideas。它会根据用户的目标、历史和 Context，自己琢磨还有什么事情可以继续做，然后主动提问，要不要试一下。

比如扎克伯格和女儿一起玩 Civilization，Muse 先帮他们做了一套游戏攻略。

做完以后，它自己又想到，可以把这个攻略继续扩展，顺便加入不同文明的历史知识。于是它主动问扎克伯格，要不要继续做。扎克伯格说可以，它就接着往下干。

这个功能直接让我感受到了 Aha Moment。

就像那天我和朋友交流 Muse 的时候说，我觉得这玩意开始有一点眼力见了。它会主动观察用户，然后说这些事它可以帮忙干。

这个功能特别有意思。

因为今天很多人使用 AI 最大的问题，已经不是 AI 不够强，而是根本不知道 AI 还能帮自己做什么。

我们打开一个聊天框，还是要自己想 Prompt，然后决定让 AI 做什么任务。

但如果 Agent 已经足够了解我们的 Context，它其实可以反过来更主动的发现问题、推进任务。

然后在这个基础上，我想解释下为什么我觉得 Muse 有可能成为 AI 时代的微信。

其实现在大家应该都已经感觉到了，AI 时代很多产品真正发生的变化，可能根本不是把 AI 塞进产品里。

新一代 AI 产品，和之前移动互联网时代产品最大的不同是，它的受众用户除了人，还有 Agent。

所以产品从设计的第一天开始，就得把 Agent 当成非常重要的用户。

现在行业里的 Agent，本质上还是一个 Single-player Game。你有你的 Agent，我有我的 Agent，大家彼此之间基本独立。

但扎克伯格觉得，后面这个状态会彻底发生变化。

他提到一个 Fleet 的概念。简单理解，就是一个人的 Muse 如果发现了某种特别好的用法，其他 Muse 也可以从这些匿名化的经验里学到东西，然后再推荐给适合的用户。

这样一来，用 Muse 的人越多，每个人手里的 Muse 理论上也会变得越来越好。

再进一步，Agent 和 Agent 之间可以直接互动。

因为 Personal Agent 本身就有用户的 Context。某种意义上，它已经是数字分身了。

那两个 Personal Agent 为什么不能自己交流？

举一个非常简单的例子。

比如我下个月准备去内蒙古看秋景，想找一个摄影师。今天我要自己去小红书搜索，去微信里问朋友，或者到处找合适的人。未来可能完全不一样。

我的 Muse 知道我要去内蒙古，也知道时间、预算，以及我喜欢什么样的摄影风格。于是它可以去整个 Agent Network 里找。

另外一个人的 Muse 知道自己的主人刚好是摄影师，那几天有时间，价格也合适，过去拍过的作品风格我也喜欢。两个 Agent 可以先初步沟通。

这个时候，所谓社交网络就不再只是人主动刷 Feed、加好友、发消息了。可能变成每个人背后都有一个 Agent。

这些 Agent 带着人的 Context、需求、关系和资源，在网络里替人寻找合适的人和机会。

这个想象空间我觉得真的很大。

微信的基本节点是人。人和人建立关系，然后聊天、发朋友圈、进群、交易。Muse 这种东西的基本节点可能依然是人，但网络里真正高频活动的主体，很可能开始出现 Agent。

或者这么讲。微信是 Human Network。Muse 的终局可能是 Human + Agent Network。

当然，一说到这里，说到 Agent 拥有我们的 Context。所有人应该都会想到同一个问题：隐私怎么办？

我这两天自己用 Muse 的时候其实也非常谨慎。

因为 Personal Agent 和 Codex 这种产品还有一个很大的区别，它为了真正理解我们，需要拿到越来越多属于我们的 Context。邮件、日历、聊天、支付、各种账号。

用到后面，它可能比绝大多数人都更了解我们自己。这确实会让人不安。

对于隐私，扎克伯格的逻辑是最好的隐私承诺，不是让用户相信平台不会看，而是技术上根本看不到。

说下他们的做法。

Meta 现在给每个人的 Muse 配了一个独立的 Secure VM。

可以简单理解成，用户的 Agent 在云端有一台相对独立的电脑，个人数据、凭证和 Agent 的操作都放在这个环境里。

接下来 Meta 还准备上线一套更强的 Confidential VM。到那个阶段，整个 VM 里的数据，包括用户和 Muse 的对话，都会进一步加密，目标是连 Meta 自己也无法读取。

这一套东西，WhatsApp 已经验证过了，隐私的问题应该是可以通过机器的方式得到解决。

还有，扎克伯格对 Muse 商业模式的设想，我觉得至少从现在来看，也挺成熟的。

因为让绝大多数人长期付费使用一个 AI，无论在中国还是美国，我感觉都没有那么容易。

扎克伯格的想法是，希望绝大多数用户最后都可以免费、大量地使用 Muse。

包括现在，Muse 还是提供了非常多的免费额度，因为他的判断是，如果 Muse 这个逻辑真的成立，那它本身就应该有能力帮用户挣钱或者省钱。

比如对一个小企业来说，Muse 可以帮你做产品、跑业务，也可以接入 Meta 的广告系统，帮用户持续运营。

只要有经济价值交换，那 Muse 就可能从中拿走过路费或者什么的呗。

所以他设想的长期商业模式，也不只是每个月向用户收一笔订阅费。更大的可能是，Agent 在帮用户完成交易、做生意或者创造收入的过程中，Meta 从里面拿很小的一部分。

而且这笔钱甚至不一定直接由用户来付，也可能会来自和用户发生交易的商家。

这个逻辑其实挺顺的。

比如我让 Muse 帮我买一张机票，或者订一家酒店。原本商家为了获得这个用户就要付获客成本，那未来它也完全可以把其中一部分分给 Muse。

挺通透的这些思考，大家有时间的话，还是强烈推荐看一看。这应该是中秋假期最值得读的一篇文章了。

text:
My takeaways from $PL upcoming launches and cadence: 

PL incremental read-through: the factory is becoming the product.
Planet just sent Pelican-12 to Cape Canaveral less than 3 months after Pelican-11 launched. Same week they opened Berlin. Easy takeaway: this is no longer “another imagery company launching cubesats but rather manufacturing AT SCALE high resolution and AI enabled satellites quicker than peers. 

1. Capacity Berlin is live. First next gen Pelican targeted before year-end. Stated scale: up to 60 Pelicans a year, roughly doubling production while SF keeps running.
That capacity is for Satellite Services, not just more PlanetScope. 

Pipeline: $4B+ identified, ~$1B near-term. Backlog ~$815M. Cash ~$865M. FY27 capex raised to $100–$115M to pull this forward.

2. Cadence The number that matters is contract-to-orbit:
•  Sweden: ~4 months from signature to launch, then handover in the quarter
•  Germany: dedicated capacity in ~2 months
•  Pelican-12: design learnings from P11 already on a pad in under 3 months
They are also splitting coasts. Vandenberg stays SSO volume (Tanager-2 + 18 SuperDoves, Oct 1). Cape gets the first Pelican onto a mid-inclination Bandwagon flight. That is a product move for mid-latitude revisit, i.e. the customers who pay for tasking.

3. Quality Launch quality looks fine: contact, first light, birds marked active. Pelican-2 commissioned in days.
The real quality test is next. P11 was a Gen 2 demo and not a commercial data bird. P12 is the updated 30 cm-class pathfinder, plus edge compute and intersat comms, on a new orbit class. If that works, pricing power. If it slips, capex and margin noise.
Watch gross margin. Q2 was 59%. FY guide is 55–57% because services mix can dilute the software-like data margins even as revenue scales.

Bottom Line- $PL is trying to industrialize a 30 cm bus fast enough to sell sovereign constellations. The last 90 days say the factory is starting to keep up with the pipeline. 

Next proof: Berlin ships a finished bird this year, and Gen 2 actually sells at a higher price.

I’m constructive under $20, but to be honest, I would require as low as a price as possible given my cost basis is <5$ for me to bite for more. That said, I’m active in options just to have an opinion on overly pessimistic days. 

Planeteers Unite! $PL 🚀

text:
The core problem with TGEs is that the market is structurally built to FOMO projects into launching at fake, unsustainable, high valuations.

Look at

- Every polymarket FDV market 
- OTC point trading nonsense
- Premarket perps
- Institutional farms
- Comparisons vs other projects
- Investors
- Teams wanting to cash out
- Teams waiting for bull markets
- Bad tokenomics

And the emergent behavior that directly follows.

It all pressures projects into making the horrible decision to make TGE their biggest moment, blow the load, and then slowly bleed out from there.

If you're launching a token--and actually trying to build something to stand the test of time--go into your TGE with eyes wide open knowing that the emergent market will pressure you into short term behavior. This is going to sound silly to anyone outside of crypto, but I'm here to tell you that you are indeed not a scammer if you launch below a 1B FDV. 

You will feel the pressure. Listen to it. If you have to, ignore it. Be honest. Setup good incentives for yourself, the community, and the project. Every project is so different, but if possible, launch your token sooner than later, and get back to building.

Nothing great is created in a day or in a year, but over a lifetime.

The token is the beginning, not the end.

跟踪了下 SN80 的最新动作。在发布第一人称数据网络 Shift 之后，团队在产业破圈、生态协同的推进节奏非常紧凑：

近期与 Verona 团队合作，在韩国KBW期间举办专项活动。具身智能需要大量实体场景支持，团队正在加速将影响力渗透进亚太开发者与硬件生态中。

值得关注的是与 SN71 的联动。简单来说，SN71就是 AI 获客智能体，与SN71合作的主要目标就是为 Shift 进行AI获客，匹配并导入全球数据采集者。

Shift 让任何人戴上设备录制日常任务，就能获得Alpha代币奖励。这是目前普通人参与具身智能基础设施最直接的路径。

考虑到海量用户的数据采集与即时结算，alpha代币的多链架构非常有必要，目前已上线 Base 和 Hood ，后期将拓展至sol、arb等更多链。

SN80 @openroboto 正在走向实体产业交付环节，在整个bittensor生态中都具有相当的差异化优势。
author: travelbai
quoted_text:
看到 SN80 推出 Shift，可以说是目前机器人赛道里极具产业落地逻辑的一步。

第一阶段SN80验证了去中心化模型竞赛的高效迭代；而第二阶段的 Shift，直接向产业链上游溯源，切入物理世界的底层数据基建。

梳理下它背后的闭环逻辑：

1、为什么是“人类第一人称数据”

具身智能最大的瓶颈，从来不是调参，而是极端稀缺的真实物理交互数据。真机采集成本极高且极易损坏。

Shift 本质是去中心化版 Figure Index：全球贡献者戴上设备以第一人称录制日常任务（装配、烹饪、收纳、工具操作）。现场不需要昂贵实体机，在工厂、家庭、工位即可超低成本、全球化起量。

像 DYNA-2 已经证实：百万小时的人类视线-手部交互数据，能让模型先建立“世界动作先验（World-Action Priors）”，再迁移到机械臂做后训练，零样本泛化能力显著飞跃。Shift 要稳定、规模化地生产这类数据。

2、独创的商业飞轮：开放数据池

这是非常具有可持续性的设计。Shift 的机制设计很务实：

• 前期：产业客户如机器人公司按需定制数据，付费享有一段时间的独占期。
• 后期：独占期结束后，符合条件的数据沉淀到公共池，赋能整个开源社区与矿工去训练更强的大模型。

如此，形成“商业数据变现 ➔ 沉淀公共资产 ➔ 喂养更强模型 ➔ 仿真和真机评测提升 ➔  吸引更多客户”的正向循环，研究进展与真实收入相互强化。

3、多链架构：打通 B 端支付与微结算瓶颈

目前其 Alpha 代币已上线 Base，未来很有机会向 Solana、Arbitrum 等链扩展，这一步非常关键：

• C 端采集者：海量碎片化任务需要极低 Gas，以满足采集者的日常提现与即时结算；
• B 端工业客户：实体企业更习惯用法币或稳定币进行结算采购，成熟 EVM/L2 生态便于承接订单托管与结算。

从单纯的算法竞赛跨入到真实物理数据供给，如果这一套跑通、执行到位，SN80 @openroboto 有机会成为 Bittensor 生态真正破圈产业的标杆案例。

继续保持关注！

author: hooeem
quoted_text:
if you’re a trader you have no idea how op adding episodic memory is to your agent.

what is this and why is it over powered?

the best traders in the world will attribute success to journalling their trades.

well that same journalling will let you create episodic memory which may well turn you from a shit trader who never learns his lessons into best trader you can become.

when you journal you should be recording:

> what did i expect the market to do?
> what actually happened?
> what was my directional bias?
> what setup did i take?
> why did i enter?
> where was my invalidation?
> how much did i risk?
> how did i size / scale the trade?
> what was my emotional state?
> did i feel fomo, fear, greed, boredom or complacency?
> did i actually follow my plan?
> why did i exit?
> what was the result?
> what did i do well?
> what did i fuck up?
> what lesson should i remember next time?

this will let you create episodic memory.

you can now tell your agent in the future:

> find every trade where i used this setup before
> show me how often it worked
> show me my average return
> show me the market conditions where it worked best
> show me the conditions where it failed
> show me the mistakes i normally make with this setup
> show me how my emotional state affected my execution
> show me similar losing trades and what went wrong
> show me similar winning trades and what i did right

and now when you go to make a trade and you journal:

> current market conditions
> directional bias
> setup
> entry
> invalidation
> risk
> sizing
> catalyst
> expected outcome
> emotional state

your agent can compare it against every similar trade you have taken before.

it can tell you the exact success rate you had with this exact setup.

it can tell you your average R.

it can tell you when the setup normally works.

it can tell you when it normally fails.

it can tell you the mistakes you repeatedly make.

it can even tell you:

“you have taken this setup 14 times before.

9 were winners.

your average return was +1.7R.

but when you entered before confirmation you lost 4 out of 5 times.”

now your agent is not just analysing the market.

it is analysing your own trading history.

every trade becomes another memory.

every mistake becomes something it can retrieve.

every successful setup becomes something it can compare against.

text:
The main problem with vibecoded games is that they're all very cool technical demos, but no one seems to be playing them. That's because most concepts for vibecoded games right now are boring and ideas people have already played. 

So I wanted to run an experiment. I wanted to see if I can make a quick vibecoded browser game that people will actually want to play.  An interesting concept that I think many people will enjoy: An SCP Mystery game.

It's called The Seventh Room.

You're Grant, a researcher at Halden Station, a small outpost of the SCP Foundation's Antimemetics Division. There are seven researchers and six rooms.

Two anomalies have got into the station:

SCP-3125 spreads as an idea. It hides inside an ordinary sentence. If you hear that sentence and understand it, you're infected. If you carry it long enough, you vanish, and everyone forgets you ever existed. One of your colleagues is already infected, and they look and sound exactly like themselves.

SCP-055 has swallowed a room. Nobody can describe it. People can only tell you what it isn't. Everyone remembers a piece, and you have to put the pieces together to find the way out.

You only have one tool: amnestics. They're memory-wipe drugs that can clear the infection, but they also scramble the memory of whoever takes them. So the person you just saved might now tell you something false about the room. You can dose yourself too, but it smudges your own notes.

So every conversation is a choice. Do you trust this person? Do you dose them? Did that sentence they just said sound slightly off?

No guns, no jump-puzzles, no crafting. You walk around, you talk to people, and you slowly realise that one of the people you were just talking to is gone and you can't remember who. Your job is to find the room before you lose your mind.

quoted_text:
7월 10일 META 아티클 분석 글 중:

먼저.. 주목할 것은...

어제 발표한 Muse Spark 1.1은 가장 똑똑한 모델이 아니다.

Artificial Analysis 지능 지수로 보면 Muse Spark는 43점. 
Claude Fable 5(60), GPT-5.5(55), Grok 4.5(54)에 한참 못 미치고 중하위권에 걸쳐 있다. 

순수 지능만 놓고 보면 메타는 아직 오픈AI, 앤스로픽 뒤에 있는 게 맞다.

다만 메타가 노린 건 1등이 아니었다. 

Muse Spark 1.1이 실제로 1위를 찍은 자리는 tool use와 agentic 벤치마크다. 

도구를 활용하고, 여러 앱을 오가며 멀티스텝 작업을 끝까지 끌고 가는 능력. 

실무에서 에이전트를 돌릴 때 진짜로 돈이 되는 구간을 골라 최적화했다는 뜻이다.

여기서 가격이 매력적이다. 

입력 100만 토큰당 1.25달러, 출력 4.25달러. 

Claude Sonnet 4.6보다 저렴하다. 

더불어 그동안 오픈소스로만 모델을 뿌리던 메타가 처음으로 자체 모델을 유료 API로 열었다는 점이 중요하다. 

토큰당 돈을 받기 시작했다는 뜻이고, 앤스로픽-오픈AI가 깔아둔 유료 모델 시장에 메타가 처음 깃발을 꽂았다는 신호.

Databricks가 코딩 작업 기준으로 만든 이 Pareto 프론티어를 보면.. 

왜 이 전략이 훌륭한 선택인지 감이 온다. 

여기 메타 모델이 직접 올라와 있진 않지만, Databricks가 뽑은 결론이 핵심을 찌른다. 

토큰 단가는 실제 비용의 나쁜 지표라는 것... 

모델이 클수록 오히려 토큰 효율이 좋아 총비용이 낮을 수도 있고, 프론티어 성능은 한 회사가 독점하는 게 아니라 여러 도구의 조합에서 나온다는 얘기. 

결국 이 시장은 "가장 똑똑한 한 놈"이 다 먹는 구조가 아니라, 비용-효율-활용성 함께 경쟁하는 판이다. 

메타는 정확히 이 지점을 노리고 들어왔다.

모델을 싸게 잘 만드는 회사는 여럿이다. 

문제는 이것을 어디에 연결하느냐.

메타는 페이스북-인스타그램-왓츠앱을 합쳐 하루 35.6억 명이 쓰는 유통망을 깔고 있다. 

광고 플랫폼 위에 AI를 올리면 별도의 고객 유치 비용 없이 곧바로 매출로 연결된다. 

이번 주 화요일에 이미지 생성 모델 Muse Image를 먼저 공개하고, 오늘 Muse Spark 1.1을 붙인 순서도 그래서 의미가 있다. 

이미지가 광고 소재를 만들고, 에이전트가 플랫폼 위에서 실행하는 구조.

인스타그램 하면 떠오르는 숏츠.

영상 쪽도 밀리지 않는다. 

Text-to-Video Arena에서 메타 Muse Video는 3위에 올라 Gemini Omni Flash, Seedance 2.0 바로 뒤에 붙어있다.
 
광고주가 이미지, 영상 소재를 메타 안에서 뽑고 바로 홍보하는 흐름이 완성되면, 이건 남들이 쉽게 못 따라오는 해자다.

실적이 이미 근거가 된다. 

1분기 매출 563억 달러, 전년 대비 +33%로 5년 만의 최고 성장률. 

광고 노출 +19%, 광고 단가 +12%. 

AI가 타깃팅과 소재 생산을 밀어올리면서 나온 결과다. 

다른 빅테크가 AI 수익화 경로를 아직 증명하는 단계라면, 메타는 이미 광고라는 검증된 파이프에 AI를 흘려보내고 있다는 게 결정적 차이.

우리가 인스타로 숏츠를 보다 결국 구매 페이지로 이어지는 경험은.. 메타가 그동안 어디에서 현금을 빨아 들이고 있는지 감이 온다.

text:
The next wave of tokenized stocks could come from TradFi incumbents themselves.

DTC sits at the center of U.S. securities custody and settlement and is developing a service that would let approved institutions tokenize positions already held there. Those tokens could later be converted back into traditional holdings when needed.

Because those securities are already in DTC’s system, institutions could use existing positions for onchain settlement, collateral, and lending. That creates a path for much larger balances to move onchain through infrastructure the market already relies on.

DTC’s tokens would stay within registered wallets, but its inventory could still matter for open markets. Public chain issuers could eventually use those shares to create and redeem their own tokens, giving onchain trading and lending a much larger stock inventory to draw from.

text:
if you’re a trader you have no idea how op adding episodic memory is to your agent.

what is this and why is it over powered?

the best traders in the world will attribute success to journalling their trades.

well that same journalling will let you create episodic memory which may well turn you from a shit trader who never learns his lessons into best trader you can become.

when you journal you should be recording:

> what did i expect the market to do?
> what actually happened?
> what was my directional bias?
> what setup did i take?
> why did i enter?
> where was my invalidation?
> how much did i risk?
> how did i size / scale the trade?
> what was my emotional state?
> did i feel fomo, fear, greed, boredom or complacency?
> did i actually follow my plan?
> why did i exit?
> what was the result?
> what did i do well?
> what did i fuck up?
> what lesson should i remember next time?

this will let you create episodic memory.

you can now tell your agent in the future:

> find every trade where i used this setup before
> show me how often it worked
> show me my average return
> show me the market conditions where it worked best
> show me the conditions where it failed
> show me the mistakes i normally make with this setup
> show me how my emotional state affected my execution
> show me similar losing trades and what went wrong
> show me similar winning trades and what i did right

and now when you go to make a trade and you journal:

> current market conditions
> directional bias
> setup
> entry
> invalidation
> risk
> sizing
> catalyst
> expected outcome
> emotional state

your agent can compare it against every similar trade you have taken before.

it can tell you the exact success rate you had with this exact setup.

it can tell you your average R.

it can tell you when the setup normally works.

it can tell you when it normally fails.

it can tell you the mistakes you repeatedly make.

it can even tell you:

“you have taken this setup 14 times before.

9 were winners.

your average return was +1.7R.

but when you entered before confirmation you lost 4 out of 5 times.”

now your agent is not just analysing the market.

it is analysing your own trading history.

every trade becomes another memory.

every mistake becomes something it can retrieve.

every successful setup becomes something it can compare against.

the more journalling the more episodic memory. the more episodic memory the more wins.

okay, I’m actually going to share a @bot with you guys soon so you can steal this.

text:
MIT says 95% of company AI projects made zero dollars.

I read that twice.

Then I saw what the employees were doing behind their bosses' backs, and it made total sense.

When this report dropped, the internet already had its headline. AI is a bubble. The hype is over. Companies wasted billions on chatbots that don't work. AI stocks sold off the same week.

So I went and read what MIT actually counted.

They studied more than 300 public AI projects, interviewed people at 52 companies, and surveyed 153 senior leaders. Together, companies had poured $30 to $40 billion into AI.

95% of those projects showed zero impact on profit. Only about 5% of the custom tools companies built ever made it out of testing and into real daily work.

That part of the headline was true.

Then I kept reading, and the report flipped on me.

Only 40% of those companies had bought an official AI subscription for their staff. Workers at more than 90% of them were using AI every day anyway. Their own ChatGPT accounts. Their own Claude subscriptions. Paid for themselves, invisible to IT.

MIT calls it the shadow AI economy.

One story in the report explains the whole thing. A corporate lawyer's firm spent $50,000 on a special tool for analyzing contracts. She drafts in ChatGPT instead. The expensive tool spits out stiff summaries she can't change. ChatGPT lets her push back until the draft is right.

So the thing that failed was the $50,000 version. The $20 version was working the whole time.

The company tools mostly died for a boring reason. They can't learn. You correct them on Monday and they make the same mistake on Tuesday. And homemade tools did far worse than bought ones. Tools from outside specialists worked about two thirds of the time. Tools companies built themselves worked about a third of the time.

That was last summer. So I pulled this year's numbers, fully expecting companies to have fixed it by now.

They haven't.

In June, PagerDuty surveyed 1,250 office workers at companies making $500 million or more a year. Two out of three said they had used AI at work even though they believed their company didn't allow it. At companies with more than 1,500 employees, it hit 72%.

Deloitte's 2026 report shows companies finally started handing out official AI. The share of workers with approved tools jumped from under 40% to about 60% in one year. But among the people who got them, fewer than 60% use them in their daily work. Same as the year before.

Put those two side by side. Companies are finally paying for AI. Workers keep breaking the rules to use their own.

Now the fine print, because these numbers get abused in both directions.

MIT's report is preliminary, not peer-reviewed. It's built on interviews and surveys, not company earnings, and it measured results roughly six months after launch. Plenty of projects take longer than that to pay off. Zero profit impact doesn't mean zero value either. A tool can save your team ten hours a week without ever showing up on the earnings report. And PagerDuty sells software for managing exactly this problem, so they had a reason to go looking for it.

But strip all of that away and one thing survives.

Everyone shared this report as proof that AI doesn't work.

A year later, it reads like proof your employees figured AI out before your company did.

quoted_text:
Tokenized assets were the only major crypto sector that grew over the past year.

While DeFi, AI, infra, DePIN and memecoins all lost market cap, tokenized assets increased 267%, from $2B to $7.5B.

I think the key point is that this growth came from issuance iykyk.

Gold built the initial base, its price increased nearly 20%, while tokenized gold holdings roughly doubled from 524K to more than 1M ounces.

But equities created the biggest structural shift.

A year ago, precious metals represented almost the entire openly traded tokenized asset market. By June 2026, that share had fallen to 68%.

Tokenized stocks and ETFs went from almost zero to 23% of the sector.

By token count, the market is already concentrated:

– @bitget | rStocks: 568 tokens, 37%

– @Ondo: 406 tokens, 27%

– @xStocksFi: 183 tokens, 12%

– @RobinhoodApp: 94 tokens, 6%

– @DinariGlobal: 82 tokens, 5%

rStocks and Ondo alone account for nearly two-thirds of all tokenized stocks.

What surprised me most is how quickly exchanges are entering this market.

– @binance launched bStocks in June and reached 46 tokens.

– @Gate followed with gStocks in July and reached 63.

Of course, token count alone does not tell me which issuer will win. I care more about liquidity, asset backing, redemption, regulation and distribution.

But it does show where platforms expect demand to move.

My soft prediction is that tokenized stocks will take a larger share of the RWA market through the rest of 2026, while the gap between issuers becomes wider.

Platforms with exchange distribution and deep liquidity should grow faster than issuers that only offer a large catalog.

I am not trying to gain exposure to every RWA-related token.

I am focusing on the issuers and infra with real distribution, reliable backing and growing secondary-market liquidity.

The sector was also the most-listed category on CEXs in H1 2026.

What started mainly with gold is now expanding into stocks, ETFs and other financial assets.

For me, the next signal is whether users continue trading and holding them after the launch incentives disappear.

text:
前两天我们部队牺牲了一名侦察连的侦察飞手。

我的中国战友。

他不远万里来到乌克兰，为了心中的信念，抵抗俄罗斯的侵略！

他和我住过同一个安全屋。
一起吃饭，一起体能训练。
老哥喜欢唠嗑。喜欢看美女。

分开几周就突然听到噩耗听不能接受的。

他是我们部队牺牲的第一名外国人。

前两天还生龙活虎，还碎碎念呢。突然人就没了，特别难以接受。

找到英雄遗体的时候他们遭受到了酷刑，没有透露部队的情报。 敌人泄愤式砍断他的脖颈。

北方军区司令知道了这个事情，第一时间慰问了我们。

并且和所有中国人士兵说，他接受不了外国人死亡，这是乌克兰人的战争，你们每个人都有美好的未来，没必要为不属于你们的战争牺牲在这里。如果有大家想离开，他完全可以理解。并且帮助大家安全离开。  哪怕签了合同也可以离开。这是一次重大的失误。  和他一起牺牲的是我们二连的最好的侦察飞手。

我们没有人选择离开，决心为牺牲的战友报仇。

直到乌克兰土地上不再有俄罗斯的侵略者。

也许哪天我或者其他战友也会留陆续的留在这片土地上。

但不要悲伤我的朋友，这是我们选择的路，我们接受的结果。

为了更美好的世界。正义必胜。

quoted_text:
Nubank rumoured to acquire Monzo for ~$13b. But who gets the 💰? My usual breakdown below 👇

Investors are likely to share a huge $9.3b of profits combined, on $1.9b invested. This represents a 5.8x blended, across 11 priced rounds. 🤑 The Founders & team will share about ~$2.0b.

This is a super win for a company that had to take a down round mid-2020. My takeaways below:

1) Passion Capital's absolute home run 👑

@eileentso and Passion led each of Monzo's first three rounds. They also kept following-on in almost every round after that. The Seed alone will return nearly 200x!

Across the three seed rounds they led, that's ~$1.6b of proceeds on ~$18m invested. Legendary.

2) Two huge absolute $ winners: Goodwater and Thrive 🏆

Goodwater led the Series C in Nov-17, at a $330m post. It will return over 20x the money. That round will generate the most absolute $ of all rounds at ~$2.0b. 📈

Thrive led the Jul-17 Series B round at $100m post money valuation, and is now looking at a cool~50x on its investment.

Two amazing good calls within a few months of each other.

3) The crowd did great 🙌

Monzo raised three crowdfunding rounds, including the famous "£1m on Crowdcube in 96 seconds" in 2016. 

Those customers-turned-shareholders are sitting on ~35-80x of profits!

Probably the second best-performing retail investment in UK tech history, after Revolut's own crowdcube campaign (where investors are now sitting on 1,000x+ paper gains).

4) Buying the dip paid off 📈

The Jun-20 down round (Novator, Nikesh Arora) came in at a ~$1.7b post money valuation. Interestingly, this is below the 2019 price. Back then, everyone thought Monzo might not make it. That round will returns ~5.9x and about $1.6b.

5) The latest growth rounds: good, not great 😐

The Series H (ADQ, Tencent, Coatue) and Series I (CapitalG, GV, Hedosophia) make ~2.5x each.

For the Series H specifically, after almost five years: respectable, not spectacular.

6) Team & Founders 🧑‍🤝‍🧑🫂

Firstly: mega congrats to @tomblomfield, TS Anil and the whole team. This would be an incredibly outcome and it is definitely one to be celebrated.

The team here will do very well, despite Monzo raising eleven rounds and diluting meaningfully. I estimate that Founders & ESOP will get about 15% of the outcome, or ~$2.0bn.

one of the more interesting new primitives i’ve seen is @perpdotcity turning live data feeds into perpetual markets

prediction markets work well when something eventually resolves yes or no, but most of the world doesn’t move like that

shipping traffic, power prices, company revenue and compute demand are constantly changing

they already have a perp tracking the number of cargo ships and tankers moving through the Strait of Hormuz, updated every 15 minutes using live AIS data

so instead of betting on whether the strait closes by a certain date, you can trade the actual flow of traffic as sanctions, convoys and geopolitical risk change it

this is basically financializing the rate at which reality is moving

if the data is reliable and liquidity comes, every valuable information stream becomes its own market

feels like one of those ideas that looks niche until there are thousands of them

text:
everyone's sharing motion graphic videos that Opus 5.5 made, and it's genuinely insane

everyone says they created it with "one prompt", but my one prompt video looked mid

so i went through a bunch of these videos to see how they were actually made, and found the workflow that works

here's how to generate pro level motion graphic videos w/ opus:

1. get reference videos to direct from -> https://t.co/CibWaQ6c9Q

pick 1-2 videos whose style you want and tell opus to match them. naming a style works way better than describing one

without a reference, opus falls back to its default look: centered text, gradient background, everything fading in

that's why so many of these videos look the same. a reference gives it the pacing, the type and the transitions to copy

2. install @HyperFrames_ or @Remotion so opus can build the video

both let opus write every scene as code and render it straight to mp4. no video editor

without one, opus can only describe a video or hand you a rough html page you have to screen record

with it, every frame is exact, and when you ask for a change it edits one line and re-renders instead of starting over

3. install @21st_dev for high quality components in the video

real buttons, cards and UI components made by design engineers, instead of whatever opus invents on the spot

without it, opus draws your product UI from scratch and it looks off. wrong spacing, placeholder boxes, fake-looking buttons

anyone who's used good software can feel it in a second, and the whole video reads as cheap

4. steps 1-3 were context + setup. now dump all of it into opus

your brand (logo, colors, fonts), screenshots of your real product, the reference video, and a quick braindump of how you see the video

then ask for 3 storyboard variants

without this, opus guesses your colors, your font and what your product even does. the video could be for any startup

with it, it could only be yours. and 3 variants means you pick a direction instead of fixing the first idea it had

5. pick the storyboard you like

ask for one still frame per scene before anything moves. fixing a storyboard is way cheaper than fixing a render

without this step, you only find out scene 4 is wrong after the whole thing is animated, and every fix means re-rendering. a still frame takes seconds to change

6. let claude cook

then give notes like a director: "slow every zoom to 0.7x", "hard cut here", "push in on the button"

without notes, the first render is usually 80% there, and that last 20% is what makes it look pro. vague notes like "make it better" get random changes. camera words get exactly the change you want

everyone has the same model. the context you give it is what makes it look pro

text:
Bitcoin has never really had a liquidity problem. @Starknet 

The bigger problem has always been what you can actually do with that liquidity without taking Bitcoin out of the picture entirely.

That’s what makes Starknet’s BTCFi direction interesting to me.

With strkBTC, the idea is to bring Bitcoin into Starknet’s DeFi environment so that BTC doesn’t have to sit idle. 

Instead, that capital can potentially move through different parts of the ecosystem from being used as collateral and liquidity to lending, liquidity provision, and other onchain strategies And that shift matters.

There’s a big difference between Bitcoin simply being held and Bitcoin becoming usable capital. 

The underlying asset doesn’t change, but its role does. Instead of having value locked away in a wallet, that same BTC can potentially participate in financial activity across multiple protocols.

I also find the privacy angle worth watching.

The goal isn’t just to make Bitcoin accessible within another ecosystem. 

Starknet approach also includes options around shielded transactions, giving users more control over how much of their balances and transfers are exposed publicly onchain.

That adds another layer to the whole BTCFi conversation.

For years, Bitcoin has been incredibly valuable, but much of that value has remained relatively passive. 

BTCFi is essentially asking a different question: what happens when Bitcoin becomes more programmable, composable, and usable across a broader financial ecosystem?

That’s where I think the interesting part begins.

The amount of Bitcoin liquidity already available isn’t the main story. 

The real opportunity is building the infrastructure that allows that capital to do more while still retaining its connection to Bitcoin.

strkBTC is one piece of that puzzle.
So I’ll be watching Starknet’s BTCFi ecosystem closely  not simply because it brings BTC somewhere new, but because it explores what Bitcoin liquidity could look like when it becomes genuinely productive onchain.

author: sterlingcrispin
quoted_text:
I'm seeing a lot of fund managers and old heads on the timeline disparage meme coins for being stupid, valueless, or not solving problems. But those accusations misunderstand what meme coins are and why they're thriving. 

Young people can't see a path to wealth or home ownership. Most americans think its unlikely the younger generations will reach a better standard of living than their parents. We don't believe in the american dream anymore. These days most young people want to become famous streamers, not get into STEM careers. And everybody is extremely addicted to their phones with absolutely obliterated attention spans. 

We have a chronically online adhd population who doesn't believe in the american dream looking for a way out. And so get rich quick opportunities have emerged to satisfy those desires. It's been a perfect storm of forces combining with Robinhood, the pandemic stimulus, the GameStop short squeeze, the '21 crypto bull run, and the normalization of sports gambling all screaming in our faces that there's a chance to escape the 9 to 5.

Meme coins were around before all this, but they've emerged from these conditions and cemented themselves into a growing number of peoples minds as a path to Make It. The fact that they're absolutely stupid is a feature, not a bug. It helps them reach the most number of people.

The most successful meme coins are the lowest common denominator. The top 100 meme coins are overwhelmingly cats, dogs, or farm animals of some kind. They communicate to the majority of young people who are chronically online dopamine junkies with executive function disorders. Coin has dog.

The meme coin market cap is over $122 billion. Doge is worth more than Volvo. If you're doing fundamental value analysis on commodities and securities this is all going to look like the world has gone crazy. And in a lot of ways it has. But meme coins haven't tricked the world into valuing them. Rather, societal conditions demanded they existed. We've collectively summoned them into existence through our adhd, chronically online lives, and distrust of the american dream.

I think it's easy to argue that those conditions shouldn't exist. We shouldn't be online so much, we shouldn't be indoors by ourselves so much, we shouldn't be locked in to low wage jobs, houses shouldn't be so expensive, etc. But being angry at meme coins is focusing on a symptom not the cause.

If you're working a poorly paying job you hate, looking at houses shitter than your apartment with mortgage payments twice your rent, you've got student loans you'll never be able to pay off, and no way of saving or investing to out pace inflation, then trying to gamble your way out of hell on dog coins might sound pretty good.

Beyond that, young people do value memes. And it makes sense that if you create some viral post you should get paid for it, not just the platform you posted it on who's using it to boost their advertising revenue. Are meme coins the best medium to monetize viral ideas and put some valuation on them? Maybe not. But the fact that it can give creators some stake in their success, rather than just big corporations like youtube or facebook, seems like an opportunity. 

The fact that meme coins have so much volatility is dangerous and it's really easy to lose your money. But that's also what gives you a chance at making it. 

Norm MacDonald has a couple of good quotes on gambling, and these three are the TLDR if you aren't reading all this 

"I remember a psychiatrist once telling me that I gamble in order to escape the reality of life, and I told him that’s why everyone does everything."

"As long as the red dice are in the air, the gambler has hope. And hope is a wonderful thing to be addicted to."

"Yeah man, they call gambling a disease, but it's the only disease where you can win a bunch of money."

There’s a spot to stack tokens before they even go live, with APY hovering in the double digits.

And yes, I'm looking straight at @MeridianCapDAO.

But farming is just the trailer. The real plot twist is where that capital goes once the yield party ends.

Meridian’s plan is to build a treasury on @RobinhoodCrypto Chain that buys $MCD, owns its trading liquidity, earns fees, and reinvests them.

Here’s how it works.

During its five-day Genesis campaign, users deposit supported assets to share 500,000 gMCD. Each pool charges a 2–5% deposit fee, which goes to the treasury.

The remaining principal can be withdrawn anytime.

IMO, your eventual rewards need to cover the deposit fee and exit costs before you’re ahead.

You’re farming gMCD, which is non-transferable and redeemable for MCD after launch.

Once farming ends, a 24-hour conversion window lets participants exchange some or all of their remaining deposited principal for gMCD at $0.10. It’s optional and first come, first served, capped at $1.5 million overall and $100,000 per wallet.

Instant redemption gives you 10% of the MCD amount. A full seven-day vest gives you 100%. Everything forfeited is burned.

What does the treasury do?

Meridian plans to spend half its Genesis raise buying MCD daily over 60 days. The other half is paired with those purchases in treasury-owned liquidity pools.

LP fees and MCD trading taxes help fund further liquidity and buybacks. Some purchased tokens will also be burned.

The potential is straightforward: turn launch interest into liquidity that keeps earning.

The catch? Fundraising isn’t recurring profit.

If trading activity fades, revenue can shrink while the initial buyback budget runs down. MCD placed in liquidity also remains available for trading; it hasn’t been burned.

So, what’s your take, will MCD’s ponzinomics be the next big winner?

NFA. DYOR.

Huge fan of crypto rails for tcg / collectibles and build in the space myself, but just wanted to clear up misunderstandings around buyers premiums.

The 20-22% buyers premium on auctions should be baked into the final price / comp of the card (when you look at price history on alt/cardladder, they report on final price). For tcg, all these auction houses pay most of the buyers premium to the sellers. E.g. auction house I work with pays me 115% of hammer, buyer pays 120% of hammer so I get 96% of the final sale.

In addition they provide
- dedicated rep that responds within 20 mins almost 24/7, who each have their own ops team to resolve issues quickly

text:
Just a small blurb of why I don’t do server racks anymore. 

I did for quite a while. But one thing that scared me away from them, and it’s my own fault as well, is I kept frying a motherboard. Multiple times on the same case. And it scared me off them. 

Now that’s the first part. Second part is they’re expensive. 

If you go server racks, you now need:

- Chassis ($3-400 x N GPU machines)
- Server rack (~$300)
- Rails per chassis (~$150 per machine)

And that’s on the low end if you’re not doing backplane stuff, which I wasn’t. 

So ballpark roughly ~$14-1600 just to house your machines. 

Versus…. My $100 Classico Max which fits 14 HDDs and $300 for my Meshify 2 XL, and another $100 for the mining rig frame. 

If you have unlimited budget, sure. Go do true HPC, get a server rack, and have fun. But I wasted enough money on parts and broken motherboards that instead I’ll do maybe not what’s “normal” but what I find interesting, fun, and enjoyable because it’s reliable for me. 

Also I didn’t have a space that could support a backplane either, so if I went beyond 4 GPUs, I can’t do much about it.

text:
A customer has paid us $128 under protest. I supervise complaints for an internet provider, and I have processed the $128 part.

The protest arrived in the same email. We are keeping it in case he ever disputes having paid under protest.

His installation cost $64. We charged it twice. He attached a photograph of the router to demonstrate how much internet we had installed. There was 1 router. I could have confirmed this from his account, but I like customers to participate.

Before we got back to him, his payment went through. His complaint closed automatically.

He replied to the closure email: "I paid because you said you'd cut me off."

That was helpful. We had asked him to do something, explained the consequences, and he had done it. I added the exchange to our training materials. Several staff members had been struggling to get customers to follow instructions.

He opened another complaint. This closed because the disputed invoice was settled. He attached the original complaint to a fresh complaint and gave it a different name. For a while we were dealing with a router fault. We offered to send a technician. He declined because the router worked.

I have rarely seen such agreement between a customer and our records.

By the following month he had devised a solution. He would deduct $64 from his next bill. That way the amount would remain outstanding until somebody read what he had written.

Collections read it. They replied with a link to financial support.

He wrote back that he could afford $64. Within 6 minutes they had arranged a call to discuss why he hadn't paid it.

He asked them to speak to Complaints. I explained to Collections that his complaint had been resolved. They thanked me for checking. He was copied in, so he could see departments working together.

He paid the arrears, leaving 1 cent unpaid.

This was more promising. He paid the rest, kept his service running and sent a message explaining that the cent represented his continuing objection. He even gave it the original case number. It was now the most thoroughly documented cent in the company.

Every morning he logged in to check it was still there.

I began to understand how much this meant to him. The money had become secondary. He wanted an acknowledgment that something remained unresolved. Here was a customer asking for something we could provide at almost no cost.

I approved a goodwill credit of 1 cent.

The account balanced. The complaint closed. He received an email thanking him for giving us the opportunity to put things right.

He called within 3 minutes. He wanted the cent put back.

I explained that reversing a goodwill gesture would require me to charge him money he did not owe. I take that sort of thing very seriously.

He offered to put that request in writing.

I let him. Our complaints team had spent 2 months being accused of taking his money without permission. At last we had his permission.

text:
This accident disclosure just revealed what everyone in the industry already knows: the curator business model doesn’t work without someone continuously paying for integrations and LP deals.

DeFi was supposed to cut out the middleman. Yet with this model, you can end up stacking as many as five layers of fees: integrator fees, curator fees (sometimes charged both onchain and offchain as “consulting” fees to asset issuers), LP fees, and middleware fees (we do not expect it will be forever free, right?).

Unlike Web2, DeFi enables extreme composability. Eg if you are not on Amazon, you can not sell your product. But in DeFi, you can be fully integrated everywhere via smart contracts. In this environment, owning the underlying protocol and its economics can be far more valuable than the potential benefits of broader distribution deals.
author: DeFi_Made_Here
quoted_text:
A lot of people reached out asking about paid integrations, how protocols can even compete, and what the growth perspectives are for Fluid in this case. Here are some thoughts:  Paying for integrations and exclusivity is simply part of growth strategy and business development. That's completely normal. A lot of people just do not know about this and think that eg Morpho is getting all integrations by default.   Morpho has a very strong backing and an excellent BD team, but they won't be able to pay for every integration forever. There is also the question of alignment between partners.

Eg the Coinbase deal reportedly cost ~7x less than the Robinhood deal, yet Coinbase accounts for more than 60% of Morpho's TVL and has been a major contributor to $morpho becoming the highest-valued lending protocol. This high valuation helped to finance the deal with Robinhood, which is a direct competitor to Coinbase. CB is well known for their negotiating skills, so it'll be interesting to see what happens when they revisit that relationship.

I also agree with what @euler_mab said about tokens. A new token can open many doors. Like Euler, we chose not to launch with a new token and instead continued with the token from the previous protocol from 2021. That decision came with limitations, but when one opportunity closes, others emerge.

That said, I think it is too early and naive to think that there is a clear winner among lending markets and I am very excited about @0xfluid future.

But how can Fluid or other lending markets navigate in this space, which has turned into enterprise sales controlled by suits?  First of all, the world is pretty big. There are thousands of banks, funds, fintechs with trillions of dollars in AUM. The pie is large enough for multiple winners.

Second, Fluid has a fundamentally superior architecture, and I know that matters to sophisticated integration partners. Instead of integrating separate lending markets, DEXes, and other financial primitives, partners can integrate once and access everything through a single stack while working with one team.

On top of that, Fluid is the only protocol with equivalent deployments across EVM, Solana, and soon Sui - three different VM ecosystems. (And what if I told you there are more VMs to come?)

Powered by Fluid  We have had great success with our first distribution partner - @jup_lend powered by Fluid. A $2B TVL protocol with plenty of growth ahead.

We'll be launching additional white-label deployments with traditional asset managers, exchanges, neobanks, and other partners in the near future.

We don't have the luxury of paying for every integration, but we can win partners through better technology, white-glove support, and predictable economics instead of fee switches or curator fees that can be turned on at any time.

DEX v2 - it is a shame that we keep delaying it despite announcing it a year ago, but we have it ready and we will launch it sooner rather than later.

DEXes generate roughly 16x more fees per $1 of TVL than lending markets, so this will be a major focus for us this year.

There are plenty of other things I'd love to share, but every time I do, another market-wide armageddon seems to happen, forcing us to delay or reprioritize launches.

So this time, let's just wait for the launches themselves.

Stay Fluid 🌊
